Female Lavender jobfish (Pristipomoides sieboldii) attain a remarkable ultimate total length of 79.0 centimeters [Li = 79.0 centimeters], a size that positions this deepwater eteline snapper among the larger members of its genus in the Indo-Pacific region. This maximum length was derived from extensive fish surveys conducted across the Hawaiian Archipelago, where specimens of this size are most frequently encountered on slopes between 150 and 300 meters depth. The body mass of such a fully grown female is considerable, field measurements indicate an asymptotic wet weight of 6820 grams [Wwi = 6820 grams], a value that reflects the robust, deep-bodied morphology typical of the species. In contrast, the onset of reproductive capability occurs much earlier in the life cycle, with females reaching sexual maturation at a total length of 39 centimeters [Lp = 39 centimeters]. This length at puberty corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 826 grams [Wwp = 826 grams], indicating that females invest substantial somatic growth between the initiation of gonadal activity and the attainment of their asymptotic size, a pattern common among long-lived, iteroparous tropical snappers.

The early developmental stages of the Lavender jobfish are characterized by a remarkably small initial size, with hatching occurring after a brief incubation period of 5 days [ab = 5 days] at a stable water temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C]. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries a wet weight at birth of only 0.00029 grams [Wwb = 0.00029 grams], a minute mass derived from the small, pelagic egg diameter of approximately 0.82 millimeters. This initial body size is consistent with the lecithotrophic phase typical of lutjanid larvae, during which the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves. Following yolk-sac resorption and the onset of exogenous feeding, the actively growing larva enters a prolonged pelagic phase, dispersing widely in oceanic currents before settlement. The extreme fecundity of this species compensates for this diminutive and vulnerable early life stage, with a maximum reproductive output estimated at roughly 16,400 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 16,400 eggs per day] under optimal thermal conditions of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], a rate scaled from fecundity data in related eteline snappers.

Life-history theory predicts considerable longevity for a deepwater snapper reaching nearly 80 centimeters in total length, and field observations of Lavender jobfish confirm this expectation. The maximum lifespan of this species has been estimated at 40 years [am = 40 years] based on otolith increment analyses conducted at 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], a temperature representative of the mesophotic depths they inhabit. This longevity is comparable to that of other Pristipomoides species such as Pristipomoides filamentosus, which also exhibits slow growth and extended senescence in similar thermal environments. The combination of a 40-year maximum lifespan with a relatively large ultimate size allows females to accumulate numerous reproductive events over their lifetimes, even though the initial maturation at 826 grams [Wwp = 826 grams] occurs several years post-hatching. Such a life-history strategy, characterized by delayed maturity and high adult survivorship, is typical of fish occupying stable, low-predation deepwater habitats where energy allocation favors persistence over rapid turnover.

Reproductive ecology in the Lavender jobfish involves a prolonged spawning season, with gravid individuals observed throughout much of the year in the central Pacific. Laboratory-based estimates of the maximum reproduction rate indicate that each individual spawns multiple batches over the annual cycle, and this is corroborated by histological examination of ovarian tissue, which reveals asynchronous oocyte development and the potential for continuous gamete production. A single female nearing her ultimate total length of 79.0 centimeters [Li = 79.0 centimeters] can produce an enormous number of pelagic oocytes per spawning event. The batch fecundity has been extrapolated from congeneric species such as Lutjanus carponotatus and adjusted for the larger body size of Pristipomoides sieboldii, yielding approximately 16,400 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 16,400 eggs per day] at 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C]. This high fecundity offsets the considerable mortality faced by the tiny, 0.00029 gram [Wwb = 0.00029 gram] yolk-sac larvae as they drift in the plankton.

Comparative analyses within the family Lutjanidae reveal that the Lavender jobfish exhibits one of the more extreme combinations of small offspring size and large adult body mass among the eteline snappers. The hatchling wet weight of 0.00029 grams [Wwb = 0.00029 grams] stands in stark contrast to the 6820 gram [Wwi = 6820 gram] asymptotic mass of a fully grown female, yielding a mass ratio exceeding twenty million to one. The corresponding length at puberty of 39 centimeters [Lp = 39 centimeters] is reached after several years of growth, at a point when females weigh roughly 826 grams [Wwp = roughly 826 grams], or just over twelve percent of their ultimate mass. This pattern aligns with theoretical expectations for species inhabiting relatively stable, food-limited deepwater environments where slow growth and deferred reproduction are favored. The incubation period of 5 days [ab = 5 days] at 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C] is brief relative to that of many tropical lutjanids, though it is consistent with the elevated metabolic rates associated with small pelagic eggs. Maximum recorded longevity in this species of 40 years [am = 40 years] ensures that even with a delayed onset of maturity, females have ample opportunity to contribute to the next generation across numerous spawning seasons at a temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C].
